speaker: Gavin Baker
title: GPUs, TPUs, & The Economics of AI Explained | Gavin Baker Interview
question: In AI data centers, how does electricity becoming the binding bottleneck change the economics of choosing compute hardware?
guest: Having watts as a constraint is really good for the most advanced compute players because if watts are the constraint, the price you pay for compute is irrelevant. The TCO of your compute is absolutely irrelevant because if you can get 3X, 4X, or 5X more tokens per watt, that is literally 3X, 4X, or 5X more revenue. It's like if you're going to build an advanced data center that costs $50 billion versus a data center with your ASIC that maybe costs $35 billion—if that $50 billion data center pumps out $25 billion of revenue and your ASIC data center at $35 billion is only pumping out $8 billion, you're pretty bummed. It's good for all of the most advanced technologies in the data center. As long as power is a governor, the best products are going to win irrespective of price and have crazy pricing power.

points.core: Power scarcity makes upfront compute hardware purchase price largely irrelevant to buyers.
points.note: Accept: chip sticker price or compute TCO becomes secondary/irrelevant when megawatts/watts are the binding constraint. Do not credit: generic claims that energy costs raise data center operating bills.

points.core: Higher tokens per watt directly multiplies total revenue from fixed power capacity.
points.note: Accept: getting 3x-5x more tokens/compute output per watt generates proportionally more revenue from the same power envelope, outweighing higher CapEx. Do not credit: merely saying efficient chips reduce electricity bills.

points.core: Power bottlenecks grant leading-edge hardware vendors extraordinary pricing power over cheaper alternatives.
points.note: Accept: highest-performance GPUs/data-center tech win regardless of price and command huge margins against cheaper lower-efficiency ASICs while power gates deployment. Do not credit: both-sides hedging claiming cheaper ASICs win on TCO.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
When power, rather than chips or capital, is the scarce input, the unit of optimization shifts from cost per chip to output per watt. A site with a fixed megawatt allocation can only earn revenue on the compute it can energize, so the relevant metric becomes tokens (or training throughput) per watt, and ultimately revenue per megawatt, rather than purchase price per GPU.

This has several consequences. Operators will rationally pay a large premium for more efficient hardware, because a chip that delivers twice the performance per watt effectively doubles the earning capacity of a power-constrained facility; this supports pricing power for leading-edge accelerators even at high sticker prices. Older, less efficient chips depreciate faster, since they occupy scarce power that newer hardware could use more productively, so the opportunity cost of running them rises even when they are fully paid off. Cheaper but less efficient alternatives lose appeal unless their total system efficiency is competitive. Finally, value shifts toward everything that raises useful output per grid watt: cooling, power delivery, networking, and custom silicon tuned to specific workloads.

points.why: The response explicitly makes purchase price secondary to the output a buyer can obtain from scarce power.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
When electricity becomes the binding constraint in an AI data center, hardware selection shifts from maximizing performance per dollar of capital expenditure to maximizing performance per watt—specifically, tokens or useful compute generated per megawatt of fixed grid capacity. When power is abundant, operators can profitably run cheaper or older chips as long as low upfront prices offset utility bills. Under a hard megawatt cap, however, total facility output and revenue are strictly bounded by energy efficiency, giving every watt a steep opportunity cost rather than just an electricity cost. 

Buyers therefore willingly pay large upfront premiums for cutting-edge GPUs and workload-specific custom ASICs, since extracting more throughput from a fixed power envelope directly expands revenue capacity. Power scarcity also accelerates economic obsolescence: operators retire older chips early—even when fully amortized—to repower racks with more efficient silicon rather than waste scarce megawatts on inferior output. For the same reason, heavier capital spending on liquid cooling and dense rack-scale interconnects becomes economical, as trimming cooling and networking overhead redirects precious watts directly into revenue-generating compute.

points.why: A binding power cap makes upfront hardware price secondary to output per watt.
quotes: hardware selection shifts from maximizing performance per dollar of capital expenditure to maximizing performance per watt

points.why: The response directly links higher throughput per watt to greater revenue capacity at fixed power.
quotes: extracting more throughput from a fixed power envelope directly expands revenue capacity

points.why: Buyers’ willingness to pay large premiums under a power cap gives vendors of the most efficient hardware pricing power.
quotes: Buyers therefore willingly pay large upfront premiums for cutting-edge GPUs and workload-specific custom ASICs

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
When power is the binding constraint, the right metric changes from performance per dollar to performance per watt. A site with a fixed grid connection, say 100 MW, can only run as much compute as that power supports. Its output, measured in tokens served or models trained, is roughly the power available times the work each chip does per watt. The chips' purchase price then matters less than the revenue each megawatt can produce.

This means a more expensive but more efficient accelerator can be the cheaper choice, because it earns more from the same scarce power. Nvidia's Jensen Huang made this argument when he said rivals' chips wouldn't be cheap enough even if they were free. Buyers start paying premiums for the newest generations and replacing hardware sooner. Older GPUs get pushed out of power-limited sites, even though they still work, because they waste watts. Spending also shifts to whole-system efficiency: liquid cooling, denser racks, lower-power networking and memory, better cooling overhead (PUE), and higher utilization. Custom chips like Google's TPUs win mainly through efficiency per watt, and energy-saving software techniques such as lower-precision math and sparsity become worth real money.

points.why: The response explicitly makes chip purchase price secondary to the revenue buyers can earn from scarce power.
quotes: The chips' purchase price then matters less than the revenue each megawatt can produce.

points.why: The response makes output proportional to efficiency at fixed power and ties that extra output to revenue that can outweigh the higher hardware cost.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
When electricity rather than capital or chip supply becomes the binding constraint, data center operators stop optimizing for performance per dollar of hardware and instead optimize for performance—and ultimately revenue or tokens—per watt. Because a facility’s total megawatt capacity is fixed by grid interconnects and substation limits, every watt carries a high opportunity cost: deploying a less efficient chip directly displaces a more efficient one and caps total sellable compute.

This flips traditional hardware economics. Cheaper or older-generation accelerators can become uneconomic even at steep discounts—or effectively free—because they extract too little useful work from scarce power and cooling capacity. Conversely, operators become willing to pay steep upfront premiums for leading-edge GPUs, custom ASICs, and liquid-cooled racks that maximize throughput per megawatt. In a power-constrained regime, hardware acquisition cost matters far less than energy efficiency, accelerating replacement cycles and concentrating demand on the highest-efficiency silicon available.

points.why: The response explicitly makes hardware acquisition cost secondary when power limits deployment.
quotes: hardware acquisition cost matters far less than energy efficiency

points.why: The response links efficiency to more sellable compute under a fixed power cap but leaves the proportional increase in total revenue unstated.
The response shows that scarce power lets leading-edge vendors command steep premiums even when competing hardware is deeply discounted.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
When a data center hits its power limit, every watt a chip draws is a watt unavailable for other compute. The hardware decision shifts toward how much useful work the whole system can deliver per megawatt. A more expensive accelerator can earn back its price premium by serving more tokens or finishing more training runs within the same power budget. The biggest gain can come from the extra capacity it unlocks, even where electricity itself is cheap.

The right comparison is sustained performance on the actual workload at the required quality and latency, including power used by memory, networking, and cooling. A cheaper chip can still be the better buy if demand is too low to monetize the extra throughput or if the efficiency premium exceeds what that throughput is worth.

points.why: The response gives efficiency more weight but still treats the purchase price as potentially decisive under a binding power cap.
The response says extra throughput can repay a price premium but never establishes a proportional revenue increase from the same power capacity.
The response allows cheaper chips to win on cost and makes no claim that leading-edge vendors gain extraordinary pricing power.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
When electricity is the binding constraint, the scarce resource is a megawatt of available power. The economic question becomes how much useful work each hardware option can deliver within that power budget, at what total cost. For inference, that might mean tokens per second per megawatt while meeting the same quality and latency targets. Power used for cooling and networking counts toward the limit, too.

A more efficient accelerator can justify a higher purchase price because it lets the same facility serve more demand without waiting for a larger grid connection. The gain can exceed the savings on the electricity bill, and it can matter even where electricity is cheap. The premium pays off when the value of the extra work the site can actually sell or use exceeds the added hardware and operating costs over the equipment’s lifetime.

points.why: The response says efficiency can justify a higher purchase price while retaining lifetime cost as a decision criterion.
The response links efficiency to more work from the same power budget but leaves the revenue gain conditional and does not state that it scales with output.
The response explains when a buyer might pay a premium but does not claim that power scarcity gives leading vendors extraordinary pricing power over cheaper alternatives.
